content: 1. Individuals with a negative Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) should not undergo 36 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). National authorities should define high tuberculosis (TB) incidence and transmission settings based on local epidemiology and the transmission dynamics of both TB and HIV. 2. Six months of daily isoniazid monotherapy is the standard treatment for latent TB infection in both adults and children, regardless of whether they live in high or low TB incidence countries. Systematic reviews have consistently demonstrated its preventive efficacy. 3. No controlled clinical trials have directly compared the efficacy of 9 months versus 6 months of isoniazid monotherapy. However, re-analysis of historical U.S. Public Health Service trials from the 1950s and 1960s showed that the benefit of isoniazid increases progressively when administered for up to 9–10 months, after which the benefit stabilizes. 4. A systematic review and meta-analysis of three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in people living with HIV in high TB prevalence settings demonstrated that continuous IPT reduces the risk of active TB by 38% more than 6 months of isoniazid. The effect was more pronounced in individuals with a positive TST, showing a 49% reduction in active TB and a 50% reduction in mortality. In those with a negative TST, the reduction in TB incidence was 27%, but this was not statistically significant. 5. A systematic review and its 2017 update showed that 3–4 months of daily rifampicin plus isoniazid has similar efficacy and safety to 6 months of isoniazid monotherapy. This regimen can be considered an alternative in low TB incidence settings. A new review comparing the effectiveness of rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months versus isoniazid for 6 or 9 months in children found no clinical disease in either group, using radiographic findings as a proxy for active TB. 6. A systematic review of a 3-month weekly regimen of rifapentine plus isoniazid compared to isoniazid monotherapy included four RCTs. These trials analyzed subgroups of adults with and without HIV and children/adolescents. No significant difference in TB incidence was found in an intention-to-treat analysis, but a per-protocol analysis showed lower rates of TB or death in participants receiving continuous isoniazid. The 3-month weekly regimen was administered under direct observation in all studies. 7. The selection of treatment regimens should consider patient characteristics to ensure initiation and completion of therapy. All treatment options can be self-administered, and an RCT demonstrated that self-administered 3-month weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid is not inferior to directly observed therapy. However, direct observation requirements may hinder implementation. 8. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) emphasized that shorter regimens are generally preferred by patients, clinicians, and program managers. They also noted that the benefits of all treatment options outweigh potential harms. 9. For latent TB infection (LTBI), 9 months of isoniazid is considered equivalent to 6 months in low TB incidence countries with strong health infrastructure. However, 6 months is preferred due to better feasibility, resource requirements, and patient acceptability. 10. The recommendation for at least 36 months of daily isoniazid monotherapy for people living with HIV is conditional, depending on TB epidemiology, health infrastructure, and program priorities. 11. For infants and children under 15 years, 3 months of daily rifampicin plus isoniazid is strongly recommended due to its safety profile, higher treatment completion rates compared to isoniazid monotherapy, and the availability of child-friendly fixed-dose combinations. 12. There is no significant evidence linking the use of isoniazid or rifamycins for LTBI treatment to bacterial resistance to TB drugs. However, active TB disease must be excluded before initiating preventive treatment, and regular follow-up is required to identify early cases of active TB during treatment. 13. Rifampicinand rifapentine-containing regimens should be prescribed cautiously to people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) due to potential drug-drug interactions. These regimens should not be used with protease inhibitors or nevirapine. However, they can be safely administered with efavirenz-based ART without dose adjustment. 14. Individuals receiving LTBI treatment should be monitored monthly for adverse events, including hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and hypersensitivity reactions. Patients should be educated about symptoms of adverse effects and advised to contact healthcare providers immediately if symptoms occur. 15. Vitamin B6 supplementation is recommended for individuals at risk of peripheral neuropathy, such as those with malnutrition, chronic alcohol dependence, HIV infection, renal failure, diabetes, or those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. 16. Adherence to and completion of preventive treatment are critical for clinical benefit and program success. Interventions to improve adherence should be tailored to the needs of specific risk groups and local contexts. 17. Preventive treatment for household contacts of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) patients may be considered based on individualized risk assessments and clinical justification. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low-quality evidence. 18. Close clinical observation and monitoring for the development of active TB disease are required for at least 2 years, regardless of whether preventive treatment is provided to MDR-TB contacts. 19. Preventive treatment for MDR-TB contacts should be individualized after assessing exposure intensity, source case certainty, drug resistance patterns, and potential adverse events. LTBI testing is required before initiating treatment. 20. The GDG judged that the potential benefits of targeted preventive treatment for MDR-TB contacts outweigh the harms, despite uncertainty about efficacy due to the lack of RCTs.
